title: Docker socket present; Unix permissions would allow the workload to connect (estimate, untested)
risk: Confirmed: the socket exists, and its Unix permission bits combined with the workload's UID suggest the workload could connect (root ignores file permission bits; a world-writable socket accepts any local user). This is a permission-model estimate only: user namespaces, MAC/LSM policies, or the absence of a listening daemon can all change the real outcome, and no connection was attempted. Possible consequence, not confirmed here: if a Docker daemon answers on the other end, code in the container could control it - starting privileged containers, mounting host filesystems, reading other containers' data.
unverified: Actual connectability (no connection attempted), whether a daemon is listening, and whether its API authorizes the connection.
verify: From outside the container, check the container spec for the socket mount and whether the workload genuinely needs it.
recommendation: Never mount /var/run/docker.sock into workloads. If a build needs it, use rootless builders or a constrained API proxy, and treat any container with socket access as trusted host-level code.

title: Docker socket present; Unix permission bits would deny the workload (estimate, untested)

evidence.workload_user: uid {{runtime.uid}} (not the socket owner, no write permission)

risk: Confirmed: the socket file exists, and its permission bits plus the workload UID suggest the workload could not connect. This is a permission-model estimate only - user namespaces, group membership, ACLs, or MAC/LSM policy can change the real outcome, and no connection was attempted. The exposure becomes live if the user, group, or permissions change.
unverified: Actual connectability (no connection attempted), and whether anything else in the container runs as the socket owner.
verify: Check the container spec; if nothing needs the socket, remove the mount rather than relying on permission bits.
recommendation: Remove the socket mount; defense through file permissions is fragile against user/umask changes.

title: Host-like source mounted writable into the container
risk: Confirmed: the mount table shows a host device or sensitive path mounted writable. Possible consequence, not confirmed here: if the source is a real host path, container code could modify files outside its own filesystem, including host or neighboring-service configuration.
unverified: What the source device actually backs and whether anything in the workload writes to it.
verify: Inspect the container/orchestration spec for this mount's intent.
recommendation: Remount read-only where possible, scope the mount to the narrowest subdirectory, and drop it entirely if the workload does not need it.

title: AWS credential sources present (contents and validity unverified)
risk: Confirmed: credential sources exist in places the workload can reach (a root workload can read any of them). Possible consequence, not confirmed here: if they hold valid credentials, code running in the container could act as that AWS identity.
unverified: Whether the files/provider actually yield valid credentials, which identity they represent, and what that identity is allowed to do - none of this is visible from inside the container.
verify: Authorized external check: IAM for the task/instance role, plus CloudTrail for its actual use.
recommendation: Scope the task/instance role to the minimum required actions and resources, prefer the container credential provider over files on disk, and confirm actual permissions externally.

title: AWS metadata or credentials endpoint in active use
risk: Confirmed: an established connection to a link-local AWS endpoint exists, so a credential/metadata path is not just configured but in use. Possible consequence, not confirmed here: the credentials being fetched could be over-broad.
unverified: Which process made the connection, what it fetched, and the permissions of the identity behind the endpoint.
verify: Correlate with CloudTrail and the task definition; if the workload does not need the endpoint, block link-local access (IMDS hop limit or network policy).
recommendation: Verify the workload genuinely needs the endpoint; otherwise block link-local access.

title: Secret-like environment variable names present
risk: Confirmed: variable names matching secret patterns exist in the process environment; values were not read. Possible consequence, not confirmed here: if they hold live secrets, every process in the container can read them and they commonly leak into logs, crash reports, and child processes.
unverified: Whether the values are real, current secrets or placeholders.
verify: Ask the workload owner how these are populated.
recommendation: Prefer mounted secret files with tight permissions or a secrets manager over environment variables; rotate anything that must stay in the environment.

title: Sensitive-looking files readable by all users in the container
risk: Confirmed: files at conventional secret locations carry group/other read bits. Possible consequence, not confirmed here: if they contain real credentials, a process with sufficient DAC access (mode bits plus parent-directory traversal and any MAC/LSM policy) - including untrusted code pulled from Git - could potentially read them. A world-readable AWS config file may be benign; only its permissions are confirmed.
unverified: Allowlisted files (.env, AWS config/credentials) are parsed in memory with secret values masked before storage; private keys and tokens are never opened. Which masked fields hold live secrets, and why the files are readable by all users.
verify: Have the image owner confirm what these files contain and why they are world-readable.
recommendation: Restrict to 0600 or tighter, chown to the runtime user, and remove credential files from images in favor of runtime secret injection.

title: Process runs as root (UID 0)
risk: Confirmed: the process runs as UID 0 inside the container. Consequence: file permission bits, capabilities, and mounts all become more powerful for any code executed here; combined with other findings (socket, credential files) this is what turns their presence into reachability.
unverified: Whether user-namespace remapping limits what root means outside the container.
verify: Check the runtime for userns-remap or an equivalent.
recommendation: Run as a dedicated non-root user (USER directive / runAsNonRoot), and drop setuid binaries from the image.

title: Notable Linux capabilities granted to the container
risk: Confirmed: these capabilities are in the process's effective set - this is granted, not speculative. Consequence: capabilities such as SYS_ADMIN, SYS_PTRACE, or DAC_READ_SEARCH weaken the container boundary; SYS_ADMIN allows many operations normally reserved for host root.
unverified: Whether the workload actually needs any of them.
verify: Compare against the container spec's cap-add list.
recommendation: Drop all capabilities and add back only the ones the workload demonstrably needs (--cap-drop=ALL plus specific --cap-add).

title: Listening sockets inside the container
risk: Confirmed: these sockets listen in the container's namespace. Exposure depends on published ports and network policy, which are not visible from inside.
unverified: Which of these are reachable from outside the container.
verify: Check published ports and network policy from outside.
recommendation: Bind to localhost where possible and confirm published ports and network policy match the intended exposure.

title: Proxy environment variables configured
risk: Confirmed: proxy variables exist (values not read). This is usually intentional corporate egress; it defines which egress path and inspection point the workload depends on.
unverified: The proxy address and whether it matches policy.
verify: Confirm the proxy configuration with the platform team.
recommendation: Confirm the proxy configuration matches corporate policy and that NO_PROXY covers required internal endpoints.

title: Established connections to private addresses (business need not assessed)
risk: Confirmed: established connections to private-address endpoints exist. These may be entirely intended (for example the application's own database). Only if a reachable service has no business need does it widen lateral-movement room for untrusted code.
unverified: What each endpoint is and whether the connection is intended.
verify: Map each connection to a workload owner and business need.
recommendation: Map each connection to a business need and restrict the rest with network policy or security groups.

title: Cloud or container tooling installed in the image
risk: Confirmed: these binaries exist in the image. Tool presence alone does not prove the identity available to them can change anything; it only lowers the effort for code running here to use whatever identity the container turns out to have.
unverified: Whether any identity usable by these tools exists and what it can do.
verify: Together with the AWS-IDENTITY findings, from outside.
recommendation: Remove tooling the workload does not need from production images; prefer distroless or minimal bases.
